_note: SF neighborhood content, districts 8-10. See d1-d4.json for the sourcing rule.

neighborhoods.name: Russian Hill
neighborhoods.intro: Russian Hill rises steeply above Polk Street, with view flats and a small number of detached houses on some of the sharpest grades in the city. Lombard's crooked block sits at its northern end.
near: The crooked block and hillside overlooks
A dense retail and restaurant corridor
The cable line runs over the hill

neighborhoods.name: Nob Hill
neighborhoods.intro: Nob Hill is the historic summit above downtown, built around grand co-operatives, hotels and Grace Cathedral. Detached houses are almost unknown here; the market is apartments and co-ops.
near: The Gothic Revival cathedral at the summit
Three cable lines cross the hill
A formal square at the crest

neighborhoods.name: Lower Nob Hill
neighborhoods.intro: Lower Nob Hill covers the blocks below the crest toward downtown, dense with pre-war apartment buildings. It is an apartment and condominium market with essentially no single-family stock.
near: BART and Muni Metro a short walk south
Retail and restaurants to the west

neighborhoods.name: Telegraph Hill
neighborhoods.intro: Telegraph Hill climbs to Coit Tower on stairways and narrow lanes, with cottages and view flats clinging to the eastern slope. The stock is small-scale and unusual by city standards.
near: The summit landmark and its bay views
Garden stairways down the eastern face
North Beach retail at the foot of the hill

neighborhoods.name: North Beach
neighborhoods.intro: North Beach is the city's Italian quarter, dense and highly walkable, built around Washington Square and the Columbus Avenue corridor. Its market is flats and condominiums rather than detached homes.

neighborhoods.name: Financial District & Barbary Coast
neighborhoods.intro: The Financial District is the city's commercial core, with high-rise residential above street level and almost no detached housing. What trades here is condominiums in towers and converted buildings.
near: BART and Muni Metro through the district
Market hall and ferry terminal on the Embarcadero
The retail core a short walk west

neighborhoods.name: North Waterfront
neighborhoods.intro: The North Waterfront runs along the Embarcadero north of the Ferry Building, built largely from converted piers and warehouses. It is a condominium market with no single-family stock.
near: A waterfront promenade along the bay

neighborhoods.name: Union Square
neighborhoods.intro: Union Square is the city's retail core, overwhelmingly commercial with hotels and high-rise residential above. It appears in the neighborhood map as a district rather than a residential area.
near: The city's principal department stores and boutiques
BART, Muni Metro and two cable lines

neighborhoods.name: Civic Center
neighborhoods.intro: Civic Center is the government and performing-arts precinct, built around City Hall and the plaza. Residential stock is limited and almost entirely apartments and condominiums.
near: Opera, symphony and ballet around the plaza
BART and Muni Metro at the plaza
The formal square before City Hall

neighborhoods.name: Tenderloin
neighborhoods.intro: The Tenderloin is one of the densest neighborhoods in the city, built almost entirely of pre-war apartment buildings and single-room occupancy hotels. Its market is apartments and condominiums.
near: BART and Muni Metro at the southern edge
A neighborhood green with a playground

neighborhoods.name: Mission District
neighborhoods.intro: The Mission is the district's dense, walkable core — one of the sunniest parts of San Francisco and among its best connected, with two BART stations and the Valencia and 24th Street corridors. The stock ranges from intact Victorians to flats above shopfronts.
near: Two of the city's densest independent retail corridors
Two BART stations within the neighborhood

neighborhoods.name: Potrero Hill
neighborhoods.intro: Potrero Hill catches more sun than almost anywhere in the city, with south-facing slopes, quieter streets and long views toward the bay. The stock is a mix of Victorians, mid-century homes and newer infill.
near: Bay and downtown views from the upper blocks
A hillside park with skyline views

neighborhoods.name: Bernal Heights
neighborhoods.intro: Bernal Heights is a hill of cottages and small houses south of the Mission, the most family-scaled neighborhood in the district. Cortland Avenue serves as its village main street and the grassland summit gives 360-degree views.
near: A grassland summit with views in every direction

neighborhoods.name: Central Waterfront & Dogpatch
neighborhoods.intro: Dogpatch and the Central Waterfront are former industrial blocks by the bay, heavily redeveloped over the past two decades. The market is condominiums and converted buildings rather than detached homes.
near: A bayfront park on the former shipyard
Restaurants and retail along the corridor

neighborhoods.name: South of Market
neighborhoods.intro: South of Market covers the broad blocks between downtown and the Mission, a mix of lofts, towers and converted industrial buildings. Detached single-family stock is essentially absent.
near: Museums and gardens at the northern edge
BART and Muni along Market Street
A small oval green at the district's heart

neighborhoods.name: Mission Bay
neighborhoods.intro: Mission Bay is wholly new construction on former railyards, built around the UCSF campus and the waterfront arena. It is a condominium market from end to end.
near: A major research and hospital campus
Muni Metro plus Caltrain at 4th & King

neighborhoods.name: South Beach
neighborhoods.intro: South Beach runs along the waterfront around Oracle Park, built almost entirely of high-rise and mid-rise condominiums. It is one of the busiest condominium markets in the city and has no single-family stock.
near: The ballpark and the bayfront promenade
BART to the north, Caltrain at 4th & King
A bayfront green along the Embarcadero

neighborhoods.name: Yerba Buena
neighborhoods.intro: Yerba Buena is the museum and convention precinct south of Market, with high-rise residential above the gardens. Its market is condominiums in towers.
near: BART and Muni Metro a short walk north

neighborhoods.name: Bayview
neighborhoods.intro: Bayview is the district's largest neighborhood and one of the sunniest parts of San Francisco, built mostly of detached houses on standard lots. It is among the most attainable single-family markets in the city.
near: A hilltop park with bay and city views

neighborhoods.name: Bayview Heights
neighborhoods.intro: Bayview Heights sits on the rise above the Bayview flats, a small pocket of homes with long views over the bay. Very little is attributed to it separately in the sales record.
near: Hilltop parkland with wide bay views

neighborhoods.name: Hunters Point
neighborhoods.intro: Hunters Point occupies the eastern waterfront around the former naval shipyard, with substantial redevelopment underway. Newer construction here is predominantly condominiums and townhouses.

neighborhoods.name: Excelsior
neighborhoods.intro: The Excelsior is a dense grid of family homes around Mission Street in the city's south, and one of its highest-volume single-family markets. The stock is mostly detached houses from the 1920s through the 1950s.
near: The city's second-largest park, to the east

neighborhoods.name: Portola
neighborhoods.intro: Portola sits on the slopes east of McLaren Park with long southern views, once the city's nursery district. It is a steady, largely detached single-family market.
near: The city's second-largest park, immediately west
Muni Metro east, freeway access nearby

neighborhoods.name: Visitacion Valley
neighborhoods.intro: Visitacion Valley lies at the city's southern edge beside McLaren Park, with modest detached homes and Caltrain at Bayshore. It is among the most affordable ground in San Francisco.

neighborhoods.name: Crocker Amazon
neighborhoods.intro: Crocker Amazon sits on the Daly City line at the city's southern boundary, with consistent post-war stock on a regular grid. It is a steady, attainable single-family market.
near: Playing fields at the neighborhood's center

neighborhoods.name: Outer Mission
neighborhoods.intro: The Outer Mission runs between the Excelsior and Balboa Park along Mission Street, with modest homes on a flat grid. It is one of the more affordable single-family markets in the city.
near: The corridor running the length of the neighborhood
BART and Muni at the western edge

neighborhoods.name: Mission Terrace
neighborhoods.intro: Mission Terrace is a small pocket near Balboa Park station, with consistent detached homes on quiet streets. It sits between the Outer Mission and the City College campus.
near: Playing fields, a pool and a stadium
The main campus to the west

neighborhoods.name: Silver Terrace
neighborhoods.intro: Silver Terrace occupies the hillside blocks above the Bayview flats, with detached homes and views east toward the bay. It is an attainable market with steady turnover.
near: Bay views from the upper blocks
Muni Metro at the foot of the hill

neighborhoods.name: Little Hollywood
neighborhoods.intro: Little Hollywood is a small pocket tucked below the freeway near the county line, with modest homes on a handful of streets. Very few properties trade here in any quarter.

neighborhoods.name: Candlestick Point
neighborhoods.intro: Candlestick Point sits on the bay at the city's southeastern corner, on the ground around the former stadium site. What trades here is predominantly newer condominiums and townhouses.
near: A state recreation area on the bay

neighborhoods.name: Sunnyside
neighborhoods.intro: Sunnyside sits on the slope below Mount Davidson between Monterey Boulevard and the freeway, with consistent detached homes and a steady market. Glen Park's BART station is a short walk east.
near: A neighborhood park and recreation center
